related_work: Ryan went back through history. In 1957, Josef Svoboda used many projectors together like a grid. Charles and Ray Eames used seven screens in a dome in 1959. Before cinema, there were huge panorama paintings. Sean Cubitt talked about even older things, like the Lascaux cave, where people looked at animal paintings by firelight, and Plato’s cave, where people only see shadows on the wall.
conclusion_future_work: This class showed me that projection and immersion are very old ideas, not new technology. For this week, I can write a short piece about the history of projection, or make a work for projection or a screen. Next week, we will learn about speculative design and planetary art, and read Benjamin Bratton’s The Terraforming.
results_discussion: I learned that “immersive” doesn’t only mean VR. Ryan said looking carefully at a painting is also immersive. Sean said even watching a fire is an immersive experience. He also said a cinema is “a dark place where people go to stare at the wall”. The big screens in Tokyo, like the 3D cat, are not projection, because the screen itself gives out light.
title: week7
introduction: This week was about projection and immersive spaces. Ryan taught the first half, and our guest, Sean , taught the second half. The main question was: is what we see a projection, or is it a screen that gives out its own light? Ryan said projection is light, something that blocks the light, and a wall.
